source.name: NordicTraits
source.citation: Niittynen, P. et al. (2026). NordicTraits: imputed species-level functional trait dataset for vascular plants of Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden. bioRxiv preprint.

traits.description: Categorizes how far seeds or propagules are typically dispersed from the parent plant.
Describes the primary agent responsible for seed dispersal.
traits.levels: Adh = fruits hooked or sticky, facilitating dispersal in the fur or feathers of animals, AirD = fruits very small and light, thereby easily carried by the wind, AirP = fruits plumed by hairs facilitating wind dispersal, AirW = fruits with wings facilitating wind dispersal, Bird = fruits with a nutritious colored tissue attractive as food of birds (or rarely mammals), Expl = fruits with active explosive/ballistic dispersal mechanisms, Myr = fruits with an elaiosome attracting ants that carry away the fruits, Passive = fruits without functional adaptations to any particular vector, Veg = predominantly vegetative dispersal by stolons, rhizomes, runners, etc., Water = fruits with spongy tissue and enhanced floating ability facilitating water dispersal.
traits.range: Adh; AirD; AirP; AirW; Bird; Expl; Myr; Passive; Veg; Water

traits.description: Indicates how well seeds float in water, affecting dispersal in aquatic environments.
traits.levels: 1 indicates that all the seeds float still after a week in still water. 0 means that all seeds sink imediately after placing them to water.

traits.description: Measures how fast seeds fall through air, influencing dispersal distance by wind.
Reflects how attractive or edible the plant is to herbivores.
Describes the overall physical structure or shape of the plant.
traits.levels: Chamaephyte = Perennial plants with buds close to the ground, protected by snow or litter during unfavorable seasons; Cryptophyte = Perennial plants with buds buried underground or underwater, surviving harsh conditions below the surface; Hemicryptophyte = Perennial plants with buds at or just below the soil surface, allowing regrowth after seasonal dieback; Liana = Long-stemmed, woody vines that climb trees or other supports to reach sunlight; Phanerophyte = Woody plants with buds exposed above ground, typically trees or shrubs; Therophyte = Annual plants that complete their life cycle in one season, surviving as seeds during unfavorable periods; Vascular parasite = Plants that attach to and derive nutrients from the vascular system of host plants, often harming them; Vascular semi-parasite = Plants that photosynthesize but also extract water and nutrients from host plants, usually without killing them.
traits.range: Chamaephyte; Cryptophyte; Hemicryptophyte; Liana; Phanerophyte; Therophyte; Vascular parasite; Vascular semi-parasite

traits.description: Specifies if the plant grows submerged, floating, or emergent in aquatic habitats.
Indicates whether the plant has woody stems or is herbaceous.
traits.levels: non-woody = herbaceous plant, semi-woody = herbaceous plant with a woody base of the stem, woody = woody plant

traits.description: Leaf Dry Matter Content: the ratio of dry mass to fresh mass in leaves.
Specific Leaf Area: the area of leaf per unit dry mass.
The concentration of carbon in leaf tissue.
The ratio of carbon to nitrogen in leaves, indicating nutrient use efficiency.
The concentration of nitrogen in leaf tissue, important for protein synthesis and growth.
The ratio of nitrogen to phosphorus in leaves, reflecting nutrient limitation.
The concentration of phosphorus in leaf tissue, critical for energy transfer and growth.
The concentration of chlorophyll in leaves, related to photosynthetic efficiency.
The typical lifespan of the plant.
traits.levels: 1 = strictly annual, 2 = biennial or at least dying after flowering (hapaxanth), 3 = short lived perennial (often hapaxanthic but may sometimes flower for additional years), 4 = long-lived perennial.

traits.description: Describes the structure and type of fruit produced.
traits.range: achene; berry; capsule; drupe; follicle; nut; other; pod; siliqua

traits.description: Indicates whether and how much nectar the plant produces to attract pollinators.
traits.levels: 1 = no nectar production (0 g sugar/m2/year) and no collectable pollen, 2 = nectar production insignificant (<0.2 g), or absent but with low but significant amounts of collectable pollen, 3 = nectar production small (0.2–5 g), or lower but with copious collectable pollen 4 = nectar production modest (5–20 g), 5 = rather large (20–50 g), 6 = large (50–200 g), 7 = very large (>200 g).

traits.description: Specifies the primary type of pollinator the plant attracts.
traits.levels: The data are given on a three-degree scale referring to the degree of dependence on pollinating animals, with subscript letters denoting the kind(s) of pollinating agents concerned: 0a = independent of pollinators, mostly or only vegetatively propagated by fragmentation or clonal growth, 0b = independent of pollinators, mostly or only pollinated by abiotic agents (wind or water; this also includes ferns and fern-allies which are not pollinated but dependent on water for fertilization), 0c = independent of pollinators, mostly or only selfing, 0d = independent of pollinators, mostly or only producing seeds by apomixis (excluding pseudogams that need pollination of the endosperm), 1 = pollination facilitated by insects, in addition to selfing (i.e. self-compatible) and/or pollination by abiotic agents, 2 = exclusively pollinated by insects (i.e. self-incompatible): 1/2a = exclusively pollinated by Hymenoptera (bees and bumblebees), 1/2ab = exclusively pollinated by Hymenoptera and Lepidoptera, 1/2b = exclusively pollinated by Lepidoptera (butterflies and moths), 1/2 = mostly pollinated by insects other than Lepidoptera or Hymenoptera (e.g. Diptera or beetles).

traits.description: Describes how long seeds remain viable in the soil seed bank.
traits.levels: The four-degree scale translates as: 1 = transient (up to one or rarely two years), 2 = short-lived (1–5 years), 3 = long-lived (5–25 years), 4 = semipermanent (>25 years).

traits.description: Indicates whether seeds require specific conditions to germinate, affecting timing of growth.
traits.levels: The four-degree scale, possibly better treated as categories, translates as: 1 = non-dormant, germinates within 10 days, 2 = non-dormant or with non-deep physiological or physical dormancy, germinates 10–30 days after sowing, 3 = with morphological, physical or mechanical dormancy, or with intermediate physiological dormancy resulting in very slow germination but independent of temperature and season (or requiring <35 days of cold stratification), 4 = with intermediate or deep physiological or morphophysiological dormancy, only germinating after at least one period of > 35 days of cold stratification.

traits.description: Measures how long seeds remain viable under storage conditions.
The mass of a seed, influencing dispersal, establishment, and survival.
Root Dry Matter Content: the ratio of dry mass to fresh mass in roots.
Specific Root Area: the surface area of roots per unit dry mass, linked to nutrient uptake.
Specific Root Length: the length of roots per unit dry mass, related to resource acquisition.
The extent to which roots are colonized by mycorrhizal fungi, aiding nutrient uptake.
Specifies the type of mycorrhizal association.
traits.levels: None = no mycorrhizal associations, AM = arbuscular mycorrhiza, AM/EM = with both arbuscular mycorrhiza and ectomycorrhiza, ArbM = arbutoid mycorrhiza, EM = ectomycorrhiza, ErM = ericoid mycorrhiza, MonM = monotropoid mycorrhiza, OrkM = Orchid mycorrhiza, PyrM = Pyrola mycorrhiza.
traits.range: AM; AM/EM; EM; EriM; EriM/ArbM; MonM; None; OrkM; PyrM

traits.description: The concentration of nitrogen in root tissue, important for growth and metabolism.
The concentration of phosphorus in root tissue, critical for energy transfer and growth.
The proportion of total plant biomass allocated to roots, reflecting belowground investment.
The maximum height the plant typically reaches, influencing light competition and dispersal.
The total surface area of a leaf, related to light interception and gas exchange.
The length of a leaf, influencing light capture and transpiration.
The average mass of a leaf, related to resource investment and function.
The thickness of a leaf, affecting light absorption, gas exchange, and drought tolerance.
The maximum depth roots penetrate into the soil, affecting access to water and nutrients.
Classifies plants into competitive, stress-tolerant, or ruderal strategies based on habitat.
traits.levels:
The Grime CRS plant strategy system.
C (Competitor) = Plants that thrive in productive, low-stress, low-disturbance environments by outcompeting neighbors for resources.
R (Ruderal) = Plants adapted to high-disturbance, low-stress environments, characterized by rapid growth and reproduction.
S (Stress-tolerator) = Plants adapted to low-resource, high-stress environments, growing slowly but persisting under harsh conditions.
Some species may exhibit mixed strategies (e.g., CS, CR, or CSR), reflecting adaptations to intermediate conditions.
traits.range: C; CR; CS; CSR; R; S; SR

traits.description: Indicates whether the plant obtains nutrients by trapping and digesting animals.
traits.levels: The ability (yes), or inability (no) to trap and digest animals.

traits.description: Describes the seasonal timing of leaf production, growth, and senescence.
traits.levels: deciduous = plants shed all their leaves seasonally, usually in response to cold or dry periods; variable = plants that can exhibit either deciduous or evergreen traits, depending on environmental conditions or species variability; evergreen = plants retain their leaves year-round, replacing them gradually.

traits.description: Indicates whether the plant can convert atmospheric nitrogen into a usable form via symbiosis.
traits.levels: The ability (yes), or inability (no) to form symbioses with bacteria capable of fixing atmospheric nitrogen

traits.description: Describes whether the plant obtains resources by parasitizing other plants.
traits.levels: none = non-parasitic species, hemiparasite = own photosynthesis but extracting water and mineral nutrients from the host, holoparasite = fully dependent on the host also for carbohydrates.

traits.description: Specifies the photosynthetic pathway used, affecting water and carbon use.
traits.levels: C3 = the most common pathway, where CO₂ is fixed directly into a 3-carbon compound. Efficient in cool, moist conditions but prone to photorespiration in hot, dry climates; C4 = CO₂ is first fixed into a 4-carbon compound, reducing photorespiration. Common in hot, sunny environments; CAM (Crassulacean Acid Metabolism) = CO₂ is fixed at night and stored as an acid, then used during the day to minimize water loss. Typical in arid-adapted plants.
